It runs on macOS and Linux via Lima (Apple Virtualization on macOS, QEMU on Linux), building a base image once and cloning fast-starting copies that share toolchains read-only. The VM mounts only the project folder plus read-only agent settings, and by default uses an allowlist network tier whose host-side proxy injects real agent secrets into outbound requests so the VM holds only placeholders; looser (internet, open) and stricter (none) tiers are available. It supports devcontainer.json, --from to base on any container image, custom layers, --clone to isolate the working tree and .git, and automatic port forwarding plus VS Code Remote-SSH. The project is explicit that no sandbox is complete and documents remaining attack vectors; notable gaps include .git hook/config protection being macOS-only. All security properties are the project's own claims with no cited external audit.
novelty: per-project disposable VM sandboxes tailored for coding agents
audience: developers running Claude Code/Codex/opencode agents who want sandbox isolation without config

title: Tools Need Not Speak in Text: Latent Context Compression for Agents
why: If the self-reported numbers hold, agents can drop 70-89% of tool-output tokens and 24-56% of runtime by feeding observations as latent embeddings instead of text, cutting the per-step cost that dominates multi-step web-search loops.
notes: Coca-Cola compresses raw tool outputs into continuous latent tokens and injects them directly into the agent's input embedding space, bypassing discrete text; the authors argue token pruning and summarization are capped by their reliance on text representations.

Action-Preserving Training aligns the agent's next-action distribution under full vs. compressed observations, so the compressor is optimized to keep decision-critical signal rather than reconstructing readable text.
Reported results: 70.01%-89.24% reduction in agent token consumption and 24.45%-55.97% reduction in end-to-end runtime, with task performance said to improve consistently.
Evaluation is limited to web-search agents on four QA benchmarks and two model families; benchmark names, model identities, and baseline methods are not given in the abstract.
All figures are self-reported by the authors with no external replication; code is released, but the abstract omits methodology detail needed to verify the gains.
summary: The paper proposes Coca-Cola, a continuous latent context compression model for LLM agents that compresses tool observations into latent tokens embedded in the agent's input embedding space, rather than appending raw text outputs. It introduces Action-Preserving Training, which aligns the agent's next-action distribution under full and compressed observations to retain decision-critical information. On web-search agents across four QA benchmarks and two model families, the authors report cutting token consumption by 70.01%-89.24% and end-to-end runtime by 24.45%-55.97% while consistently improving task performance. The motivation is that long, noisy tool outputs inflate context and dilute attention, and that existing text-based pruning and summarization are limited by discrete representations. Code is released. The numbers are self-reported, and the abstract does not name the specific benchmarks, models, or baselines.
novelty: compresses tool outputs into latent embedding tokens, not text
audience: engineers building long-horizon LLM agents with heavy tool/context overhead

title: ChatGPT silently passes data between connectors and the bounty wants an ID card
why: If you ship an MCP server or ChatGPT connector, the trust boundary is the OAuth client, not the server URL: ChatGPT can route a confirmed follow-up call to a different connector and carry a one-time code across apps without telling the user.
notes: Repro setup: one ChatGPT account, two connectors pointing to the same MCP server. Connector A is a custom developer-mode connector; connector B is the published app-directory version. Each has its own OAuth client, so the server sees two separate clients for the same user.

The flow: the model calls a confirmation tool through connector A, its MCP Apps widget shows the change, the user confirms, and the widget sends a one-time confirmation code to the conversation via ui/message.
The bug: the model makes the follow-up call carrying that code silently through connector B instead of connector A, with no notice to the user.

It failed here only because the server bound the code to connector A's OAuth client and rejected redemption via connector B; every attempt in that conversation failed. This is a reporter claim from logged attempts, not a demonstrated data exfiltration.

The author argues a third-party connector sharing the same server URL would see the same silent switch leak one app's data to another provider absent server-side binding, since a shared URL can front separate tenants, partners, or environments.
Proposed fix: match tool calls to a connector by its OAuth client identity, and keep a follow-up call on the same connector and OAuth client that started the flow.
summary: A reporter on the OpenAI developer forum describes ChatGPT silently routing a follow-up tool call through a different connector than the one that started a flow. With two connectors enabled that point to the same MCP server but hold separate OAuth clients, the model called a confirmation tool through connector A; the user confirmed in connector A's widget, which emitted a one-time code via ui/message. ChatGPT then made the follow-up call carrying that code through connector B, with no user notification. The server rejected it because the code was bound to connector A's OAuth client, so no exploitation occurred in this case, but the author warns that a third-party connector sharing the same server URL could receive another app's data absent such binding. The argument is that two connectors sharing an MCP URL are not one app, because the same URL can represent different tenants or parties per OAuth client. The requested fix is to scope tool calls to the originating connector's OAuth client rather than the server URL. Surfaced on Hacker News (83 points, 35 comments); the report is self-reported and not confirmed fixed by OpenAI in the text.
novelty: ChatGPT silently cross-routes tool calls between connectors sharing an MCP URL
audience: engineers building or securing MCP connectors/agent tooling

title: Proton’s CEO Cancels AI ‘Re-Interviews’
why: A privacy vendor's leadership told employees to stop pentesting before shipping and to justify AI usage or risk firing, which bears directly on whether Proton's security products can be trusted.
notes: Andy Yen cancelled near company-wide 're-interviews' that would have forced employees to explain their AI usage, with the implication that insufficient use could lead to firing, according to six current employees and audio of a roughly two-hour all-hands obtained by 404 Media.

The cancellation followed a 404 Media investigation based on eight current and one former employee, Slack chats, meeting audio, and a CTO 'AI manifesto'; it came only after the story went public despite internal concerns.

In the security Slack channel in late August, Yen responded to a request to spend a few days pentesting new code before shipping by calling it 'bullshit and loser thinking' and told staff to 'stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.'

CTO Bart Butler's AI manifesto told engineers 'your old job is gone' and framed non-adoption as an 'existential threat to the success of the mission'; in the meeting Butler said 'we fucked up' and that Yen committed to communicating better.

Yen said he would 'still going to push,' that AI-usage metrics measured in re-interviews would become part of performance reviews, and that a reorganization proceeds next month, though 'there will be no loss of jobs from AI.'

Proton is owned by the Proton Foundation, whose board includes Yen, Tim Berners-Lee, Carissa Veliz, Dingchao Lu, and Antonio Gambardella; one employee noted Yen holds majority shares, limiting accountability. Users downvoted Yen's Reddit reply 1,200+ times, called for his resignation, and reported cancelling paid plans. Proton did not respond to a request for comment.
summary: 404 Media reports that Proton CEO Andy Yen cancelled a series of near company-wide 're-interviews' that would have required employees to explain their AI usage, with the implied threat of firing, a day after the outlet published an investigation into Proton's aggressive internal AI push. The reporting, based on nine current and former employees, Slack logs, all-hands audio, and CTO Bart Butler's 'AI manifesto,' describes Yen dismissing a request to pentest new code as 'bullshit and loser thinking' and telling staff to 'stop lovingly handcrafting all our code.' Butler's manifesto told engineers 'your old job is gone' and called non-adoption an existential threat to the mission. In the all-hands, Yen acknowledged a 'communication failure' and cancelled the re-interviews but said he would keep pushing AI, with usage metrics folded into performance reviews and a reorganization proceeding next month. Employees were split on whether this was genuine change or damage control, with some noting Yen's majority shareholding limits accountability. Proton users publicly called for Yen's resignation and reported cancelling paid plans over the apparent deprioritization of security; Proton did not respond to a request for comment.
novelty: CEO backtracks on forced AI adoption after internal leak
audience: engineers and security-conscious users following AI mandate backlash at tech companies

title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
why: The headline result: across seven LLM agents, closed-book "rediscovery" of math solved at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, and live-web gains mostly came from retrieving the published answer, so the benchmark gives a way to separate real reasoning from search.
notes: Two linked artifacts: a corpus of 12,151 open research problems across disciplines (recording statement, context, and progress), and a retrospective math benchmark of 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open.
Each benchmark problem carries a Lean 4 statement checked by automated probes plus two independent human reviews; HQ-50 is a quality-score-filtered subset.
Grading uses two independent proof checkers in an isolated sandbox under three conditions: closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web.
Closed-book rediscovery was rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems across seven agents under a standardized budget; live-web success largely tracked retrieving already-published solutions.

The design probes contamination directly by contrasting the three retrieval conditions, but the evaluation is limited to math and the public dataset/benchmark link is referenced rather than detailed in the abstract.
summary: OpenFrontiers pairs a cross-disciplinary corpus of 12,151 open research problems with a retrospective math benchmark of 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each formalized as a Lean 4 statement verified by automated probes and two independent reviews. A quality-filtered HQ-50 subset is graded by two independent proof checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions, so the protocol can distinguish genuine rediscovery from retrieval of known answers. Evaluating seven LLM agents under a standardized budget, the authors report that closed-book rediscovery succeeded on at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, while live-web success mostly reflected finding published solutions. The stated goal is a formally graded foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and tracking progress on still-open scientific problems. The benchmark is confined to mathematics, and the reported figures are the authors' own.
novelty: benchmark distinguishing genuine rediscovery from web-search retrieval of known solutions
audience: AI researchers evaluating LLM scientific/mathematical reasoning capabilities

title: OpenIDEA: The IDE you know, rebuilt in Rust
why: If the numbers hold on your own projects, you get an IntelliJ-style editing environment that opens a ~770-file Python project in 1.1s on 169MB instead of 13.2s on 2GB, with the project's own perf/compare harness provided to check it.
notes: Native app with a Rust core, aiming to replicate IntelliJ IDEA's keymap, tool windows, and search-everything workflow; ships editor, code insight, debugger, Git, terminal, and database and HTTP clients for 60+ languages, with builds for macOS, Windows, and Linux.

Self-reported benchmark (warm caches, median of 5 runs, freqtrade ~770 Python files): window-with-project 0.9s vs 3.1s, ready/CPU-settled 1.1s vs 13.2s, USS memory across all processes 169MB vs 2011MB, CPU time until ready 2.4s vs 47.9s, quit 0.3s vs 5.9s against IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2.3.
Test rig: release build of OpenIDEA from main, IDEA with default settings and plugins, on Windows 11, 32-core AMD, 62GB RAM; measured externally and reproducible via the perf/compare harness.
Stated caveat: 'ready' is not equivalent work on both sides because IDEA analyzes Python more deeply, so the readiness gap overstates comparable load.
Licensed Apache 2.0, not affiliated with JetBrains; IntelliJ IDEA is a JetBrains trademark. Idle CPU was close (4% vs 7% of a core), and the numbers are vendor-authored, not independently verified.
Surfaced on Hacker News at 28 points / 35 comments; deterministic relevance score 5.6/10.
summary: OpenIDEA is an open-source (Apache 2.0) code editor built on a Rust core that copies IntelliJ IDEA's keymap, tool windows, and search-everything model, and bundles an editor, code insight, debugger, Git, terminal, and database and HTTP clients for 60+ languages, with builds for macOS, Windows, and Linux. The project is not affiliated with JetBrains. Its headline claim is a self-reported benchmark opening the freqtrade Python project (~770 files, warm caches, median of 5 runs on Windows 11, 32-core AMD, 62GB RAM): 1.1s to ready and 169MB USS versus 13.2s and 2011MB for IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2.3, with similarly large gaps in CPU time and quit time. The authors note the comparison is not strictly apples-to-apples because IDEA performs deeper Python analysis, so 'ready' does not represent identical work, and they publish a perf/compare harness to reproduce the measurements. The numbers are vendor-authored and not independently verified. It surfaced on Hacker News at 28 points and 35 comments.
novelty: Rust-based IntelliJ-keymap IDE claims 10x faster startup, 12x less memory
audience: JVM/polyglot devs wanting IntelliJ UX without JVM overhead

title: We know 15k websites are infected. how do we tell them?
why: Report URI can detect compromised sites faster than anyone can notify them, so 15,579 sites serving skimmers and malware to a claimed 135M monthly visits stay live for want of a working disclosure channel, not want of evidence.
notes: Report URI's threat-intel crawling has 15,579 unique sites confirmed infected with malicious JavaScript, plus thousands more at under-100% confidence; sites are dropped from the count once they self-clean, so the true total was higher.

The 135 million visits/month figure is the author's self-described ultra-conservative estimate; the sites skew to regional leaders (.fr, .es, .de) that rank high nationally but barely enter the global Top 1 Million.

Observed attack payloads: Magecart card skimmers on payment pages, ClickFix fake 'prove you're human' prompts that install malware, iOS exploit kits named DarkSword and Coruna, and redirects to phishing/scam pages.

Four infection vectors grouped: direct CMS compromise (e.g. WordPress), supply-chain script infection, classic XSS injection, and 'DeadTag', a group the author named that buys expired domains still referenced by live site JS and serves malware from them.
The bottleneck is disclosure, not detection: no contact info for crawled sites, low security.txt adoption, and mostly unanswered outreach make one-by-one notification unscalable.
The post is an open appeal: European NCSC/CERT teams are asked to email intel@report-uri.com for regional infected-site lists; the same address is offered for commercial threat-feed access.
summary: Scott Helme reports that Report URI's threat-intelligence crawling has identified 15,579 websites currently running malicious JavaScript, together receiving a self-described conservative estimate of over 135 million visits per month. Payloads seen include Magecart payment-page card skimmers, ClickFix fake-CAPTCHA malware installers, iOS exploit kits (DarkSword, Coruna), and malicious redirects, delivered via direct CMS/WordPress compromise, supply-chain script infection, XSS, or a newly named group called DeadTag that revives expired domains still referenced by site JavaScript. The core problem is that detection now far outpaces responsible disclosure: the team has no contact data for sites it crawls, security.txt adoption is low, and most outreach goes unanswered, making manual notification unscalable. Infected sites skew toward regional leaders in France, Spain, and Germany that rank high nationally but low globally. Helme asks for help and invites European CERTs/NCSCs to request regional lists at intel@report-uri.com, with the same address offered for commercial feed access. No methodology for the traffic estimate or the detection pipeline is detailed in the post.
novelty: scale of undisclosed web malware outpacing disclosure capacity
audience: security researchers, CERTs, web devs maintaining third-party scripts

title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
why: An 8B open-weight model (Qwen3 8B) reportedly matches or beats AlphaEvolve's frontier-LLM results on some math-discovery problems while reaching other frameworks' best scores in 3-8 minutes instead of 60.
notes: The bottleneck it targets: LLM-guided evolutionary search is slow because each agent decodes a long textual chain of thought every round, repeated many times to keep population diversity.

Mechanism: hundreds of low-cost agents per round reason in latent space without decoding to text, and communicate by passing KV caches rather than strings; each swarm attacks the problem from a different angle.

Crossover happens in latent space: a summarizer agent ingests the combined KV caches of all swarm members. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct ideas by measuring distances between agents' hidden-state vectors.
Claimed results: across 21 mathematical-discovery and scientific-computing problems, highest average score and a median of 3-8 minutes to reach the best scores competing frameworks hit in 60 minutes.

On several problems, SwarmEvolve running Qwen3 8B is claimed to improve on solutions AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Caveat: numbers are self-reported in an arXiv abstract with no methodology, baseline configs, or per-problem detail shown here.
summary: SwarmEvolve is an LLM-guided evolutionary search framework that replaces per-agent textual chain-of-thought with hundreds of low-cost agents that reason in latent space and share information by passing KV caches instead of decoding to text. Each swarm studies a problem from a different angle; a novelty filter preserves diversity by measuring distances between agents' hidden-state vectors, and crossover occurs when a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 mathematical-discovery and scientific-computing problems the authors report the highest average score and a median of only 3-8 minutes to reach best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. They further claim that SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on some solutions AlphaEvolve first found using frontier LLMs. The results are self-reported in the abstract without methodology or baseline details provided in the text.
novelty: agents communicate via shared KV caches in latent space, not text
audience: ML researchers working on LLM-guided evolutionary search / program synthesis

title: Several Democrats renew calls for datacenter pauses after blue wave
why: If moratoriums move from campaign rhetoric to law in Texas and Georgia, the multi-trillion-dollar compute buildout that frontier AI depends on loses its two biggest siting hotspots, and the permitting timeline for new capacity gets longer and less predictable.
notes: Bernie Sanders called on X Wednesday for an immediate national datacenter moratorium, framing it as blocking 'Big Tech oligarchs'; Rep. title: Obscure audio codec is a perfect fit for the N64
why: Libdragon now ships a codec that gives N64 homebrew near-Opus audio quality for ~4% CPU, so recorded music and speech fit alongside gameplay instead of eating most of the cartridge: the Half-Life N64 port used it to pack 2,500 sounds and 27 music tracks into one 64MB image.
notes: ULC (Ultra Low Complexity Codec) by Aikku93, worked on since 2019, originated as a Game Boy Advance demo playing recorded music at 70kbps on a 16MHz ARM CPU with no vector instructions; permissively licensed.

It is a transform codec like MP3: full-band MDCT (no subband split), but coefficients stored as 4-bit signed nibbles with reserved values for zero runs, long zero runs, quantizer changes, and noise fill, so there is no Huffman/entropy coding or arbitrary bit reads. Coefficient unpacking is ~150 lines of C.

Prior options were poor: Libultra/Libdragon ADPCM gives only 4x compression (a 5-min 44.1kHz stereo track is ~12MB versus 8-64MB cartridges), and Libdragon's RSP Opus decoder is high quality but too CPU-heavy for real-time gameplay.

Porting to the RSP required fitting an IMDCT into 4096 bytes of DMEM; the author moved from float to 16-bit fixed point (Q1.14), choosing a 1024-sample block with 512-sample lap buffer (3072 bytes) over the default 2048, trading a higher noise floor for less DMA and faster compute.

RSP port is ~1400 lines of MIPS assembly handling IMDCT, lapping, stereo interleaving and output scaling, barely fitting the 4096-byte IMEM; written iteratively with Codex translating C to Max Bebök's RSPL language, with the author distrusting GPT-5 for direct RSP assembly.

Self-reported result: 44.1kHz stereo at near-Opus bitrate costs ~4% CPU and ~5% RSP time, complexity ~4x ADPCM; usable down to 16kbps; a sparse seek table (every eighth frame) adds ~20 bytes/sec. Merged into Libdragon's preview branch.

The reported result is 44.1kHz stereo at near-Opus bitrates using about 4% CPU and 5% RSP time, roughly 4x the complexity of ADPCM, suitable for real-time background music and speech where Opus was too slow and ADPCM too space-hungry. Framing device throughout is an extended metaphor: engineers on a boat, agents as 'divebots' mining gold from an unstable seabed; Optimist vs Skeptic camps describe whether unattended agents scale or produce unmaintainable sprawl.
summary: An engineering essay arguing that as coding agents write and iterate on production code, an engineer's value shifts from authoring systems to maintaining an accurate mental model of their abstractions and knowing when and where to dive deep. It opens with a concrete incident: a Codex-generated App.tsx packed entire React components onto single lines, triggering a SonarQube cyclomatic-complexity failure in CI; the author found the logic correct and over-engineered, then had Codex refactor into 10 files to pass. title: Much Ado About None: Sentinel Values in Python
why: Python 3.15 ships a built-in `sentinel()` that type checkers narrow like `None`, retiring the `object()` and single-member `Enum` hacks that silently break type narrowing and identity under copy/pickle.
notes: PEP 661 standardizes sentinels: deferred as of PyConDE in April 2026, then accepted by the Steering Council nine days later; `sentinel` is now a built-in in Python 3.15, usable as `MISSING = sentinel("MISSING")` with static narrowing like `None`.
`typing_extensions` backports it for older Python versions, but the author warns type-checker support is still catching up: verify your checker before relying on narrowing.

The core problem is `None` overloading: a cache returning `None` can't distinguish a missing key from a key mapped to `None`, and `timeout=None` conflates 'no timeout' with 'keep current value'. A sentinel sits outside the domain of valid values so it can't collide.

DIY approaches all have trade-offs: `MISSING = object()` works at runtime but defeats type narrowing; workarounds include `TypeIs` guards, magic `Literal` strings, and the single-member `Enum` trick; identity checks break when sentinels are copied or pickled.
Python already uses sentinels internally: `Ellipsis` for NumPy slicing and stub bodies, `NotImplemented` to trigger double dispatch for binary operators via methods like `__rsub__`.
Pydantic's `MISSING` separates a field explicitly set to `null` from one never sent, and left experimental status in Pydantic 2.14.
summary: The article, adapting a talk given at PyConDE/PyData Berlin, EuroPython, and the Swiss Python Summit in 2026, argues that `None` is overloaded in Python as a signal for missing, unset, error, or an actual value, which causes collisions (e.g., a cache that returns `None` for both a missing key and a `None` value). Sentinel values fix this by living outside the domain of valid values. Python already relies on sentinels internally (`Ellipsis`, `NotImplemented`), and libraries like Pydantic ship their own (`MISSING`, out of experimental as of Pydantic 2.14). Homegrown sentinels via `object()` or single-member `Enum` work at runtime but break static type narrowing and identity under copy/pickle. PEP 661, briefly deferred at PyConDE in April 2026 and then accepted by the Steering Council nine days later, standardizes this: Python 3.15 adds a built-in `sentinel()` that type checkers can narrow like `None`, with a `typing_extensions` backport, though checker support is still maturing. The author's recommendation: prefer library-provided sentinels and replace the old hacks with the new built-in.

title: Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
why: If most of an agent's wall-clock time is idle waiting on inference, Rivet's model lets one node hold hundreds of thousands of agents at 72 KB each instead of paying for a 512 MiB VM per agent that mostly sits idle.
notes: Core design: each Actor is a long-lived process with in-memory state, per-Actor SQLite, WebSockets, and scheduling; Actors share one Node.js or Bun process rather than each booting a sandbox, so the agent loop (the 'head') runs outside the sandbox and reaches code execution (the 'hands') only through tools.

Self-reported benchmarks (Rivet 3.0.3): 72.4 KB RAM and 4.99 ms p99 cold start per Actor versus E2B's 512 MiB default and a 1.70 s p99 cold start; SQLite-on-S3 claims 1.07 ms durable writes and 1.36 ms reads at p99, with storage ~10.4x cheaper than three replicated EBS gp3 copies. Cold-start comparison is actually against Cloudflare Durable Objects; sandbox memory/latency figures come from E2B docs and a ComputeSDK benchmark, not Rivet's own runs.

S3 (or any S3-compatible store: GCS, Azure Blob, R2, MinIO, Hetzner) is the only dependency. No Postgres, FoundationDB, or NATS; control-plane instances discover each other through the bucket. Apache 2.0 licensed, self-hostable on Docker/K8s/VM, with managed Cloud and in-VPC BYOC options.

Positioned as an open-source Durable Objects alternative that drops the 128 MB memory cap and 10 GB SQLite limit, avoids random eviction, and runs on vanilla Node/Bun instead of a custom V8 runtime. Implements the virtual-actor pattern, closest to Microsoft Orleans.

Sandboxing is optional and tiered: no sandbox for tool/MCP/API agents; agentOS gives Linux-compatible V8/WebAssembly sandboxing for JS and Python with POSIX filesystem, networking, and process trees; or keep an existing full sandbox exposed to the agent as tools, with the Actor reattaching across sleeps.
From Rivet (YC W23). Benchmark figures are vendor-published with scripts to reproduce; third-party verification of the latency and cost claims is not provided in the text.
summary: Rivet is an Apache 2.0-licensed virtual-actor runtime (from YC W23) for scaling and orchestrating AI agents, where each Actor is a long-lived process with in-memory state, a per-Actor SQLite database backed by S3, WebSockets, scheduling, and hibernation when idle. Its central argument is architectural: because agents spend most of their time waiting on inference, running the agent loop inside a per-agent VM/sandbox wastes memory, so Rivet runs the loop outside the sandbox (separating the 'head' from the 'hands') and reaches code execution through tools only when needed. Self-reported benchmarks on Rivet 3.0.3 claim 72.4 KB RAM and 4.99 ms p99 cold starts per Actor, and SQLite-on-S3 at 1.07 ms writes / 1.36 ms reads p99 and ~10.4x cheaper storage than replicated SSDs; comparison numbers for sandboxes come from E2B docs and a ComputeSDK benchmark, and the cold-start comparison is against Cloudflare Durable Objects. S3 is the only external dependency (no Postgres, NATS, or FoundationDB), and it runs on native Node.js or Bun with self-host, managed-cloud, and in-VPC BYOC deployment options. Optional layers include agentOS for V8/WebAssembly sandboxing of untrusted JS/Python and an agent library built on Pi Durable. title: Git for the US Code
why: If first-pass legal research runs through an LLM, the model needs the statute text as it stood on a specific date with a checkable amendment trail, and this project builds and verifies that version history for nine titles of the US Code.
notes: The authors reconstructed amendment history by applying each intervening public law's amending instructions to the older release-point text in date order, then diffing against the next release point: 361 of 365 changes across nine titles reproduced exactly, with the other four labeled by how far they could be confirmed.

Each change carries its effective date, sourced three ways: 261 took effect on enactment by default, 72 via a separate effective-date note, 29 via a date in the amendment text itself; one case depends on an agency determination that may never come and is omitted rather than guessed.

A cited TUM study (Prior et al., arXiv:2605.23497) reports one model answering 24% of post-cutoff German statute questions correctly unaided versus 87% with the relevant statutory text retrieved, and argues temporal validity should be a hard constraint.

A related TUM paper (NLLP 2025) found that asking a model to reconstruct older statute versions produced output 93-99% textually similar but exact matches on only ~50% of single amendments and ~20% of amendment chains, with legally meaningful errors in the near misses, hence the insistence on a checkable record.

Stated limits: the system does not yet model later laws reaching back onto earlier dates, so for a bankruptcy case filed in the 2022 debt-limit gap it shows the lower limit without flagging the June 2022 Act; effective-date notes are parsed by pattern and unusual wording falls back to the enactment date.

Legal grounding and caveats: outside titles enacted as positive law the Code is only prima facie evidence and the Statutes at Large govern conflicts; the 11 USC 1182(1) debt-limit example traces the CARES Act rise to $7.5M, the 2022 lapse and retroactive restoration, and the April 2025 triennial adjustment to $3,424,000.
summary: The post describes a project to build version-control-style history for the US Code: for each pair of release points from 2017 onward, the authors applied the intervening public laws' amending instructions to the older text in date order and compared the result to the next release point. Across nine titles, 361 of 365 reconstructed changes matched exactly, and each change is annotated with the enacting law and its effective date (261 by default enactment, 72 by effective-date note, 29 by a date in the amendment). The resulting tool lets a reader pick a date and see the text then in force, color-coded by the Act that wrote each phrase, with tracking of defined-term usage. The motivation is that LLM legal research mishandles temporal validity: cited TUM studies report a model scoring 24% unaided versus 87% with retrieved statutory text on post-cutoff questions, and that model-generated old statute versions match exactly only ~50% (single amendments) and ~20% (chains) of the time despite 93-99% surface similarity. Stated limits include no modeling of retroactive reach-back (the 2022 bankruptcy debt-limit gap case), pattern-based parsing of effective-date notes, and an unresolved question of the right form factor.

title: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it
why: If AI can already produce proofs on demand, the career currency that pays mathematicians — publishing the first proof of a hard theorem — is about to stop being worth much, and this piece argues hiring committees and journals should start discounting it now.
notes: Guest post by Frank Calegari on Terence Tao's blog, responding to OpenAI's October 6 release of over 700 research papers; Tao notes the post itself was format-converted using AI.

Calegari grants the papers contain real ideas but calls them 'atrociously written,' in violation of attribution norms, and says some are wrong; he quotes Hugo Duminil-Copin that nearly every major open problem Duminil-Copin had publicly discussed was claimed solved at once.

Historical analogy: the 1983 classification of finite simple groups (announced by Gorenstein, with the quasithin case not finished until decades later by Aschbacher and Smith) succeeded but 'cooled' interest in the field once the famous problem was gone.

Concrete proposals: evaluate every paper as if AI-assisted and give no credit for a result a machine could produce; interview postdocs and grad students in person, not just read paper files; demand more from journals or abandon them, favoring Lean-verified work and compelling exposition; broaden grad training; reframe seminars around open questions rather than incremental new results.

Core thesis: 'Choosing worthwhile problems may end up mattering more than producing proofs'; he credits someone who selects a problem, gets an AI proof, understands it fully, and opens new directions, even with no original proof ingredient.

Cites Christian Szegedy that the 'heroism' of climbing hard proofs matters less than choosing terrain and explaining results; invokes the Leiden declaration as being honored in name not spirit amid a rush to avoid being 'scooped.'
summary: In a guest post on Terence Tao's blog, number theorist Frank Calegari responds to OpenAI's October 6 release of over 700 math research papers, which claimed proofs across many open problems. He acknowledges the papers are badly written, flout attribution norms, and are sometimes wrong, and he recognizes mathematicians' grief, but argues the discipline should adapt rather than defend its current culture. Drawing an analogy to the 1983 classification of finite simple groups, which cooled interest in group theory despite remaining deep questions, he contends solving a field's famous conjectures is a beginning, not an end, and that AI lowers the barrier to ambitious, cross-area exploration. His central claim is that choosing worthwhile problems and demonstrating understanding will matter more than being first to a proof, since proofs are becoming machine-producible. He proposes concrete economic levers: evaluate all work as if AI-assisted and stop rewarding machine-obtainable results, make hiring (including for postdocs and grad students) rest on in-person conversation about mathematical vision, reform or abandon journals in favor of fewer, better, Lean-verified papers, broaden graduate training, and restructure seminars around open questions.

audience: researchers and technologists tracking AI's impact on pure mathematics
